interfaces.name: Weakly stationary real-valued stochastic process
interfaces.type_shape: Real weakly stationary process with absolutely summable autocovariances, its spectral density and a finite-dimensional spectral parameter. The later fourth-order stationarity and mixing conditions strengthen this common framework; strict stationarity, linearity and zero mean are not imposed here.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Real weakly stationary process with absolutely summable autocovariances, its spectral density and a finite-dimensional spectral parameter. The later fourth-order stationarity and mixing conditions strengthen this common framework; strict stationarity, linearity and zero mean are not imposed here.

members.source_heading: Section 3.4 — spectral process and parameter framework
members.statement_original: Consider a weakly stationary real-valued stochastic process $\{X_t\}_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ with absolutely summable autocovariances and a corresponding spectral density $f:[-\pi,\pi]\to[0,\infty)$. Let $\theta\in\Theta\subseteq\mathbb R^p$ denote a spectral parameter of interest.

evidence.location: Section 3.4 — spectral process and parameter framework
Section 3.4 — spectral process and parameter framework

interfaces.name: Spectral estimating functions
interfaces.type_shape: Parameter-indexed vector of p frequency-domain estimating functions on [-pi,pi]. Theta is the parameter domain in the section setup. No bounded-variation or differentiability condition is part of this bare definition; those are recorded separately.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Parameter-indexed vector of p frequency-domain estimating functions on [-pi,pi]. Theta is the parameter domain in the section setup. No bounded-variation or differentiability condition is part of this bare definition; those are recorded separately.

members.statement_original:
Denote a vector of spectral estimating functions as
\[
G_\theta(\lambda)\equiv(g_{1,\theta}(\lambda),\ldots,g_{p,\theta}(\lambda))^\intercal:[-\pi,\pi]\times\Theta\mapsto\mathbb R^p\tag{3.1}
\]
(to be integrated with respect to $f(\lambda)$, $\lambda\in[-\pi,\pi]$)

interfaces.name: Parametric vector of spectral moments
interfaces.type_shape: General parameter-dependent spectral moment vector, using script M. It need not be the zero vector or equal theta. Its relationship to the estimating functions and true density is a separate moment condition.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: General parameter-dependent spectral moment vector, using script M. It need not be the zero vector or equal theta. Its relationship to the estimating functions and true density is a separate moment condition.

members.statement_original:
and let
\[
\mathcal M_\theta\equiv(m_1(\theta),\ldots,m_p(\theta))^\intercal:\Theta\mapsto\mathbb R^p
\]
denote a corresponding parametric vector of spectral moments.

interfaces.name: Spectral moment condition
interfaces.type_shape: Equality required at the true parameter theta0, not an identity at every candidate theta. The moment vector may be nonzero, allowing more than normalized ratio parameters.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Equality required at the true parameter theta0, not an identity at every candidate theta. The moment vector may be nonzero, allowing more than normalized ratio parameters.

members.statement_original:
As linked through the spectral density $f$, we then assume that $G_\theta$ and $\mathcal M_\theta$ satisfy the spectral moment condition
\[
\int_{-\pi}^\pi G_\theta(\lambda)f(\lambda)d\lambda=\mathcal M_\theta\tag{3.2}
\]
at the true value $\theta_0$ of the parameter.

interfaces.name: Periodogram
interfaces.type_shape: Uncentered squared Fourier transform of the full observed stretch, normalized by 2*pi*n. The imaginary unit is distinct from the block index i. The empirical sums later omit the zero Fourier frequency.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Uncentered squared Fourier transform of the full observed stretch, normalized by 2*pi*n. The imaginary unit is distinct from the block index i. The empirical sums later omit the zero Fourier frequency.

members.statement_original: Suppose data are available from an observed time stretch $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ of length $n$, and denote the periodogram as $I_n(\lambda)=(2\pi n)^{-1}\left|\sum_{t=1}^n X_t\exp(-\imath\lambda t)\right|^2$, where $\imath=\sqrt{-1}$ and $\lambda\in[-\pi,\pi]$.

interfaces.name: Empirical spectral average
interfaces.type_shape: Riemann sum over both signs of every nonzero Fourier frequency up to floor(n/2). For even n the printed range includes both -pi and pi. It is the full-data average, distinct from the non-overlapping block averages used to form SEL.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Riemann sum over both signs of every nonzero Fourier frequency up to floor(n/2). For even n the printed range includes both -pi and pi. It is the full-data average, distinct from the non-overlapping block averages used to form SEL.

members.statement_original:
Using $I_n(\cdot)$ in place of $f(\cdot)$, a standard empirical spectral average for estimating a spectral mean $\int_{-\pi}^\pi G_\theta(\lambda)f(\lambda)d\lambda$ from (3.2) is given by
\[
T_n(\theta)\equiv\frac{2\pi}n\sum_{|j|=1}^{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}G_\theta(\lambda_{j,n})I_n(\lambda_{j,n}),\qquad\theta\in\Theta,\tag{3.5}
\]
in Riemann sum form, where $\lambda_{j,n}\equiv2\pi j/n$, $1\le|j|\le\lfloor n/2\rfloor$, denote discrete Fourier frequencies and summation over $|j|$ denotes inclusion of both positive/negative frequencies.

interfaces.name: Non-overlapping (NOL)
interfaces.type_shape: N=floor(n/b) disjoint length-b blocks with their own periodograms, normalized by 1/(2*pi*b). The original construction uses only N full blocks; it does not require b to divide n.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: N=floor(n/b) disjoint length-b blocks with their own periodograms, normalized by 1/(2*pi*b). The original construction uses only N full blocks; it does not require b to divide n.

members.statement_original:
For a block length $b<n$, the data are divided into $N\equiv\lfloor n/b\rfloor$ non-overlapping (NOL) blocks/subsamples of length $b$ as $(X_{1+(i-1)b},\ldots,X_{ib})$, $i=1,\ldots,N$. The periodogram from the $i$th subsample, denoted as
\[
I_{i,\mathrm{NOL}}(\lambda)\equiv\frac1{2\pi b}\left|\sum_{s=1}^b X_{(i-1)b+s}e^{-\imath\lambda s}\right|^2,\qquad\lambda\in[-\pi,\pi],
\]

interfaces.name: Empirical spectral average
interfaces.type_shape: Block-scale spectral averages over the non-overlapping periods. Mention of full-data T_n describes the analogous construction; the numerical value of T_n is not required to compute these block averages.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Block-scale spectral averages over the non-overlapping periods. Mention of full-data T_n describes the analogous construction; the numerical value of T_n is not required to compute these block averages.

members.statement_original:
is used for a subsample-analog of the empirical spectral average $T_n(\theta)$, $\theta\in\Theta$, from (3.5) as
\[
T_{i,\mathrm{NOL}}(\theta)\equiv\frac{2\pi}b\sum_{|j|=1}^{\lfloor b/2\rfloor}G_\theta(\lambda_{j,b})I_{i,\mathrm{NOL}}(\lambda_{j,b}),\qquad i=1,\ldots,N,
\]
where $\lambda_{j,b}\equiv2\pi j/b$, $1\le|j|\le\lfloor b/2\rfloor$; thus, $I_{i,\mathrm{NOL}}$ and $b$ from blocks replace $I_n$ and $n$ in (3.5).

interfaces.name: SEL function
interfaces.type_shape: Supremum of the product of N probability weights under an estimating-equation constraint. The convention for an empty feasible set is explicitly zero. This profiles subsample spectral averages, not individual time observations or individual full-periodogram ordinates.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Supremum of the product of N probability weights under an estimating-equation constraint. The convention for an empty feasible set is explicitly zero. This profiles subsample spectral averages, not individual time observations or individual full-periodogram ordinates.

members.statement_original:
To assess the plausibility of a given value of the spectral parameter $\theta\in\Theta$, we then define a SEL function for $\theta$ as
\[
L_n(\theta)\equiv\sup\left\{\prod_{i=1}^N p_i\ \middle|\ p_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^N p_i=1,\ \sum_{i=1}^N p_iT_{i,\mathrm{NOL}}(\theta)=\mathcal M_\theta\right\},\tag{3.6}
\]
by assigning probabilities $p_i$ to the subsample periodogram statistics, $p_i\longmapsto T_{i,\mathrm{NOL}}(\theta)$, under a mean constraint $\mathcal M_\theta$.

When the conditioning set in (3.6) is empty, we may define $L_n(\theta)=0$.

interfaces.name: SEL log-ratio statistic
interfaces.type_shape: Minus twice the log of N^N times the SEL function. When the likelihood is zero, the extended-real log-ratio is infinite under the usual convention; finite-valued convergence is a theorem conclusion, not imposed on every sample.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Minus twice the log of N^N times the SEL function. When the likelihood is zero, the extended-real log-ratio is infinite under the usual convention; finite-valued convergence is a theorem conclusion, not imposed on every sample.

members.statement_original:
Analogous to parametric likelihood, we then consider a SEL log-ratio statistic as
\[
\ell_n(\theta)\equiv-2\log[N^N L_n(\theta)].\tag{3.7}
\]

interfaces.name: Mixing coefficient
interfaces.type_shape: Strong mixing coefficient uniformly over time origins and past/future events. The supremum over event pairs is encoded in the source set-builder expression inside sup_m. Strict stationarity is not required to define this coefficient.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Strong mixing coefficient uniformly over time origins and past/future events. The supremum over event pairs is encoded in the source set-builder expression inside sup_m. Strict stationarity is not required to define this coefficient.

members.statement_original: Recall that the $\alpha$-mixing coefficient of a time series $\{X_t\}$ is given, for integer $k\ge1$, by $\alpha(k)\equiv\sup_{m\in\mathbb Z}\{|\mathbb P(A\cap B)-\mathbb P(A)\mathbb P(B)|:A\in\mathcal F_{-\infty}^m,B\in\mathcal F_{m+k}^\infty\}$, where $\mathcal F_{-\infty}^m$ and $\mathcal F_{m+k}^\infty$ denote, respectively, $\sigma$-algebras generated by random variables $X_j$, $j\le m$ and $X_j$, $j\ge m+k$; see (Athreya and Lahiri, 2006, Ch. 16).

interfaces.name: 4th-order stationary series
interfaces.type_shape: Fourth-order stationarity, a uniform 4+delta moment and weighted strong-mixing summability using the same positive delta. Neither strict stationarity nor an eighth moment nor linear-process structure is imposed.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Fourth-order stationarity, a uniform 4+delta moment and weighted strong-mixing summability using the same positive delta. Neither strict stationarity nor an eighth moment nor linear-process structure is imposed.

members.statement_original: $\{X_t\}_{t\in\mathbb Z}$ is a real-valued, 4th-order stationary series such that, for some $\delta>0$, $\sup_{t\in\mathbb Z}\mathbb E|X_t|^{4+\delta}<\infty$ and $\sum_{k=1}^\infty k^2\alpha(k)^{\delta/(4+\delta)}<\infty$.

interfaces.name: Bounded variation
interfaces.type_shape: Componentwise bounded variation in frequency at the true parameter only. The assumption does not impose a uniform variation bound over a neighborhood of all theta, nor differentiability in frequency.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Componentwise bounded variation in frequency at the true parameter only. The assumption does not impose a uniform variation bound over a neighborhood of all theta, nor differentiability in frequency.

members.statement_original: At the true parameter $\theta_0\in\Theta\subset\mathbb R^p$ value, each component $g_{j,\theta_0}(\cdot):[-\pi,\pi]\mapsto\mathbb R$ of $G_{\theta_0}(\cdot)$ is of bounded variation, for $j=1,\ldots,p$.

interfaces.name: 4th-order cumulant density
interfaces.type_shape: Triple Fourier series of fourth-order cumulants with factor (2*pi)^{-3} and negative imaginary exponent. The standard cumulant notion is ambient; Assumption 3.5.1 supplies the moments in theorem applications. No Gaussian or independent-innovation simplification is inserted.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Triple Fourier series of fourth-order cumulants with factor (2*pi)^{-3} and negative imaginary exponent. The standard cumulant notion is ambient; Assumption 3.5.1 supplies the moments in theorem applications. No Gaussian or independent-innovation simplification is inserted.

members.statement_original: and $f_4(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3)\equiv(2\pi)^{-3}\sum_{h_1,h_2,h_3\in\mathbb Z}\operatorname{cum}(X_0,X_{h_1},X_{h_2},X_{h_3})e^{-\imath(\lambda_1h_1+\lambda_2h_2+\lambda_3h_3)}$ denotes the 4th-order cumulant density of the process.

interfaces.name: Positive definite
interfaces.type_shape: Positive definiteness of the sum V_theta0, not separate positive definiteness of its two contributions. Both terms and the reflected-frequency vector are retained. The second contribution need not vanish for the allowed nonlinear processes.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Positive definiteness of the sum V_theta0, not separate positive definiteness of its two contributions. Both terms and the reflected-frequency vector are retained. The second contribution need not vanish for the allowed nonlinear processes.

members.statement_original:
The $p\times p$ matrix $V_{\theta_0}\equiv V_{\theta_0,1}+V_{\theta_0,2}$ is positive definite, where
\[
\begin{aligned}
V_{\theta_0,1}&\equiv2\pi\int_{-\pi}^\pi G_{\theta_0}(\lambda)(G_{\theta_0}(\lambda)+G_{\theta_0}(-\lambda))^\intercal f(\lambda)^2d\lambda,\\
V_{\theta_0,2}&\equiv2\pi\int_{-\pi}^\pi\int_{-\pi}^\pi G_{\theta_0}(\lambda_1)G_{\theta_0}(\lambda_2)^\intercal f_4(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,-\lambda_2)d\lambda_1d\lambda_2,
\end{aligned}\tag{3.9}
\]

interfaces.name: Spectral M-estimator
interfaces.type_shape: Root of the full-periodogram estimating equation. Theorem 3.6.1 asserts existence of a consistent asymptotically normal solution sequence, not uniqueness or those properties for every root.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: Root of the full-periodogram estimating equation. Theorem 3.6.1 asserts existence of a consistent asymptotically normal solution sequence, not uniqueness or those properties for every root.

members.statement_original:
Based on $T_n(\theta)$ and the spectral moment condition (3.2), we define a spectral M-estimator $\widehat\theta_n$ as the solution to
\[
T_n(\theta)=\mathcal M_\theta.\tag{3.10}
\]

interfaces.name: Regularity conditions
interfaces.type_shape: All four neighborhood regularity conditions, including parameter derivatives through order two, componentwise Riemann integrability at theta0, integrable derivative envelopes, and nonsingularity of the moment-equation Jacobian. These supplement, rather than replace, Assumptions 3.5.1–3.5.3.
interfaces.semantic_boundary: All four neighborhood regularity conditions, including parameter derivatives through order two, componentwise Riemann integrability at theta0, integrable derivative envelopes, and nonsingularity of the moment-equation Jacobian. These supplement, rather than replace, Assumptions 3.5.1–3.5.3.

members.statement_original: suppose the following regularity conditions in a neighborhood of $\theta_0$ satisfying (3.2): (i) partial derivatives $\partial G_\theta(\cdot)/\partial\theta$, $\partial^2G_\theta(\cdot)/\partial\theta\partial\theta^\intercal$, $\partial\mathcal M_\theta/\partial\theta$ and $\partial^2\mathcal M_\theta/\partial\theta\partial\theta^\intercal$ exist; (ii) each component $\partial g_{i,\theta_0}(\cdot)/\partial\theta_j$ of $\partial G_{\theta_0}(\cdot)/\partial\theta$ is Riemann integrable for $i,j=1,\ldots,p$; (iii) $\|\partial\mathcal M_\theta/\partial\theta\|$, $\|\partial^2\mathcal M_\theta/\partial\theta\partial\theta^\intercal\|$ are bounded, and $\|\partial G_\theta(\cdot)/\partial\theta\|$, $\|\partial^2G_\theta(\cdot)/\partial\theta\partial\theta^\intercal\|$ are bounded by a Riemann integrable function $H(\cdot):[-\pi,\pi]\mapsto\mathbb R^+$; and (iv) $D_{\theta_0}\equiv\int_{-\pi}^\pi[\partial G_{\theta_0}(\lambda)/\partial\theta]f(\lambda)d\lambda-\partial\mathcal M_{\theta_0}/\partial\theta$ is non-singular.

interfaces.type_shape: All n-b+1 consecutive length-b overlapping blocks. The printed periodogram prefactor is 2*pi/b, unlike the NOL prefactor 1/(2*pi*b). Preserve the original formula and flag its normalization mismatch.

members.statement_original:
Using the spectral M-estimator $\widehat\theta_n$ in place of the true parameter $\theta_0$ (Section 3.6.1), define a collection of overlapping (OL) subsample statistics from the data $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ as
\[
\mathcal C_{\mathrm{OL}}\equiv\{T_{i,\mathrm{OL}}(\widehat\theta_n):i=1,\ldots,n-b+1\},
\]

members.statement_original:
and define the bootstrap analog of the SEL ratio $\ell_n(\theta_0)=-2\log[N^N L_n(\theta_0)]$ as $\ell_n^*(\widehat\theta_n)=-2\log[N^N L_n^*(\widehat\theta_n)]$ for
\[
L_n^*(\widehat\theta_n)=\sup\left\{\prod_{i=1}^N p_i:p_i\ge0,\ \sum_{i=1}^N p_i=1,\ \sum_{i=1}^N p_iT_{i,\mathrm{OL}}^*(\widehat\theta_n)=\mathcal M_{\widehat\theta_n}\right\}.
\]
The above bootstrap likelihood $L_n^*(\widehat\theta_n)$ uses the spectral moment $\mathcal M_{\widehat\theta_n}=T_n(\widehat\theta_n)$, based on (3.10) and the spectral M-estimator $\widehat\theta_n$, in analog to the moment $\mathcal M_{\theta_0}$ defining the SEL function $L_n(\theta_0)$ from (3.6) at $\theta_0$.

members.statement_original:
The SEL function $L_n(\theta)$ for $\theta$ leads to a natural SEL function and log-ratio for a value of the smooth function parameter $\vartheta=h(\theta)$ as
\[
L_n(\vartheta)\equiv\max\{L_n(\theta):h(\theta)=\vartheta\},\qquad\ell_n(\vartheta)\equiv-2\log[N^N L_n(\vartheta)].
\]

D6.D2: The Riemann sum weights the periodogram by G_theta.

D8.D2: The block-periodogram Riemann sum uses G_theta.
D8.D7: The periodogram and count of blocks are the non-overlapping construction.

D9.D8: The likelihood profiles weights on non-overlapping subsample spectral averages.

D16.D6: The estimating equation uses the full-data spectral average.

D17.D2: The derivatives are of the spectral estimating functions.

D17.D4: The neighborhood is around a true parameter satisfying moment condition (3.2).
